m&m's: A Benchmark to Evaluate Tool-Use for multi-step multi-modal Tasks

A tool-use planning benchmark built from 33 real, callable tools — 13 multi-modal ML models, 11 image-processing modules, 9 free public APIs — paired with real images, audio, and text instead of placeholder filenames or an LLM emulating tool outputs, so that planning error can finally be told apart from execution error across 10 LLMs, 2 planning strategies, 2 plan formats, and 3 kinds of feedback.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By early 2024, tool-use evaluation was scattered across two kinds of imperfect setups. One kind — HotpotQA, WebShop, GQA, NLVR — never provides a ground-truth plan at all, so a wrong final answer conflates two very different failures: did the model plan the wrong sequence of tools, or did a correctly-chosen tool simply fail to execute? The other kind provides ground-truth plans but can't actually execute them. ToolEmu emulates tool execution with an LLM standing in for the sandbox rather than running real tools. TaskBench assumes a list of tools is available for planning without providing any implementation of them, and instantiates its queries with placeholder input filenames like "example.png" that don't exist on disk — so a plan can look correct on paper while being untestable in practice. MetaTool, meanwhile, only considers OpenAI plugins as tools, and while ToolBench's 3,451 tools are themselves all executable, its queries are never human-verified and carry no real multi-modal inputs. The paper's own comparison table makes the gap explicit: among ToolBench, ToolEmu, TaskBench, and MetaTool, none combines real multi-modal query inputs with a fully executable toolset — m&m's is the only one of the five that checks both boxes.

A second, quieter gap sits underneath the first: even within papers that do propose planning agents, nobody had systematically compared the design choices that go into one. Should the LLM emit the whole plan in one shot (multi-step) or one action at a time (step-by-step)? Should it call tools through JSON-structured arguments or free-form Python code? Does parsing, verification, or execution feedback actually help — and does it help the same way for a 7B open model as for GPT-4? Prior systems each picked one point in this space (HuggingGPT: plan-only, no execution; ToolFormer: single-shot plan and execution; ToolLLaMA: step-by-step with self-feedback) without a shared, executable benchmark to compare them on.

// how it works

The method

m&m's formalizes a plan as an ordered sequence of tool invocations: given a tool set and a user query, a planner must produce P = [t₁({a¹₁=v¹₁}), t₂({a¹₂=v¹₂}), …], where each step names a tool and fills in its argument names and values, and a later step's arguments can reference an earlier step's output via a <node-id>.key notation.

tool-F1 = 2 · |P ∩ G||P| + |G| // F1 over the predicted (P) vs. gold (G) set of tool names in a plan — averaged over queries

The dataset itself is built by a five-stage, largely automatic pipeline. First, the authors construct a directed graph over all 33 tools, with an edge wherever one tool's output type matches another's expected input type, and sample sub-sequences (tool graphs) from it. Second, each sampled tool sequence is instantiated with a real input — an image, audio clip, or text passage sampled from the validation sets of 11 existing datasets (including ImageNet, SQuAD, Visual Genome, MagicBrush, and LibriSpeech) — rather than a placeholder path. Third, GPT-4 is prompted with the tool graph and the real input to generate two natural user queries per sequence, explicitly forbidden from naming the tools involved. Fourth, a rule-based program (not an LLM) converts each tool graph into a fully specified JSON plan — tool names, argument names, and argument values, including the node-reference notation for chained outputs — and the same JSON is mechanically transformed into equivalent Python code; GPT-4 is used only to rewrite free-text argument values (e.g., turning "a shark" into "a child-friendly book cover image of a shark") so they better match the query. Fifth, three expert human annotators independently rate every one of the 4,427 generated query-plan pairs as solving the query or not.

Of the 4,427 raw examples, 1,565 are verified correct by all three annotators (pairwise agreement rates of 74.95%, 81.43%, and 70.88%, averaging 75.75%). The authors then apply two further filters to this 1,565-example verified set: 349 examples are removed for poor execution results (e.g. an intermediate tool returning an empty or wrong output), and a further 334 are removed for over-representing image generation — image generation alone accounted for 918 of the 1,565 verified plans, so plans with more than 4 unique queries that used it were preferentially dropped to balance the tool distribution. That leaves a final, tool-balanced evaluation set of 882 human-verified, executable query-plan pairs: 70 requiring a single tool, 159 requiring two, and 653 requiring three, drawn from 317 distinct tool graphs (averaging 2.78 unique queries per graph) over 33 tools (13 HuggingFace multi-modal ML models, 11 VisProg-style image-processing modules, 9 free RapidAPI public APIs).

On top of this dataset, the paper builds a modular planning agent — implemented with Microsoft's AutoGen framework — with four components: the planning LLM, a parser, a rule-based verifier, and an executor. The paper evaluates up to 11 distinct LLMs across three axes, but no single experiment crosses all three with the full roster — each comparison runs its own model subset. Planning strategy (multi-step: emit the whole plan at once, vs. step-by-step: one action per turn) is compared across 8 models — Llama-2-7B/13B/70B, Llama-3-70B, Mixtral-8x7B, Gemini-pro, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, and GPT-4-0125-preview (Figure 5). Plan format (JSON vs. Python code) swaps in CodeLlama-34B/70B for Llama-2-70B and Llama-3-70B, again across 8 models (Figure 7). Feedback (parsing-only, or parsing plus verification and/or execution feedback on the previous turn's mistakes) is reported for 9 models in Table 3 — the 8 strategy models plus GPT-4o-2024-05-13, added in the camera-ready revision. A separate appendix reports 10+ additional plan-evaluation metrics for 6 of these models (Llama-2-7B/13B, Mixtral-8x7B, Gemini-pro, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, and GPT-4-0125-preview). Three metrics score every configuration: tool-F1 (set-F1 over predicted vs. gold tool names), argname-F1 (set-F1 over predicted vs. gold (tool, argument-name) pairs), and pass rate (the fraction of plans that execute with no error — a measure of executability, not correctness).

// what they found

The results

The paper's first finding is that multi-step planning beats step-by-step planning on tool-F1 for every one of the 8 models compared in Figure 5, though the gap narrows for the larger, more capable models (Llama-3-70B, GPT-4). GPT-3.5 shows the single largest jump, gaining roughly 21.8 points of tool-F1 when switched from step-by-step to multi-step. On pass rate, the same multi-step advantage holds for every model in that comparison except Gemini-pro, which does slightly better under step-by-step. The authors trace part of this to a step-by-step failure mode: models tend to "Terminate" early as soon as they receive positive feedback on the steps generated so far, regardless of whether the user's full request has actually been resolved.

The second finding concerns feedback, isolated in Table 3 (multi-step, JSON format), which reports tool-F1 / argname-F1 / pass-rate deltas for verification (PV), execution (PE), and combined (PVE) feedback against a parsing-only (P) baseline. Verification and execution feedback raise pass rate substantially — e.g. Llama-2-7B's pass rate climbs from 28.23% (P) by +18.14 points under PV, and Llama-2-13B's 38.10% (P) climbs by +32.99 points under PE — while argname-F1 improves by roughly 1–4 points for most models (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, already near-ceiling without feedback, barely move). But this comes at a small cost to tool-F1: for example Llama-2-13B's 42.27% (P) tool-F1 drops to 37.70% under PVE (−4.57), and GPT-3.5's 80.52% (P) drops to 77.72% under PE (−2.80) — the paper attributes this to models over-correcting and swapping out already-correct tools when told to "fix" an error.

The third finding is about plan format: on tool-F1, JSON and code generation are comparable (within 3 points) for every model except Llama-2-7B (Figure 7a), but JSON produces a much higher pass rate than code for every model in that comparison (Figure 7b) — e.g. GPT-4 reaches roughly 97% pass rate with JSON versus roughly 88% with code. The gap traces to a common code-generation failure: the model fails to correctly access a prior step's output when chaining tool calls, an error JSON's more rigid structure makes less frequent (though it still occurs there too).

Put together, the paper's practical recommendation is multi-step planning, in JSON format, with feedback — the combination that scores best overall across tool-F1, argname-F1, and pass rate on m&m's.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The benchmark construction is genuinely careful about one classic contamination path: because every query-plan pair is freshly generated (tool graph → input → GPT-4 query → rule-based plan) rather than scraped, there's no leaked test-set string for a model to have memorized. But the paper is silent on a subtler version of the same risk. GPT-4 is the sole author of every user query in the dataset and the sole rewriter of the text-generation and image-generation argument values used to instantiate a plan — and GPT-4 (as GPT-4-0125-preview, later GPT-4o-2024-05-13) is also one of the two best-performing evaluated planners on that same dataset. Nowhere in the main text, limitations, or appendix do the authors test whether a different query-generation model would change the relative ranking of planners; it's plausible that GPT-4-authored queries have a GPT-4-recognizable phrasing style that a same-family planner is disproportionately well-suited to parse. This is a stylistic self-alignment concern, not classic answer leakage, but it's exactly the kind of thing a benchmark whose data-generation model is also a benchmarked model needs to rule out, and this one doesn't.

One row-pair in Table 3 should not be quoted as measured. Mixtral-8x7B and Gemini-pro have distinct base values (tool-F1 66.79 vs 69.38; argname-F1 72.52 vs 73.37) and normally-differing pass-rate deltas, yet their six feedback deltas are byte-identical across both metrics — 1.18, −0.11, −0.04 for tool-F1 and 2.00, 1.89, 2.72 for argname-F1. Two independently-evaluated models agreeing to the hundredth on six of twelve delta cells while differing on the other six is a transcription artifact rather than a result, and the paper never flags it. It doesn't overturn the qualitative claim that verification and execution feedback help argument-name prediction and hurt tool selection — that pattern holds in the other rows — but the specific magnitudes for these two models shouldn't be relied on.

The headline tool-F1 and argname-F1 numbers also tell a rosier story than the paper's own appendix does. Table 3's GPT-4 tool-F1 of 88.46% (parsing feedback only) is a set-overlap score — it doesn't require the tools to be in the right order or their arguments correctly bound. The appendix's stricter, exact full-plan accuracy (Table 9: does the entire predicted plan, tools and argument names, exactly match the gold plan?) tops out at 71.43% for GPT-4 under multi-step planning with execution feedback — a roughly 17-point gap between "mostly picked the right tools" and "produced the literal correct plan." That gap is far starker for weaker models: Llama-2-13B's 42.27% Table-3 tool-F1 corresponds to an exact multi-step plan accuracy that never exceeds 13.83% in Table 9. A reader who only sees Figure 5/6/7 and Table 3 in the main paper would not know this collapse exists. Code generation shows the same pattern in an even sharper form: AST accuracy (exact match of the predicted code's parse tree to the reference) never exceeds 5.33% for any of the six models measured in Table 14 — including GPT-4 — even though CodeBLEU, a fuzzy similarity score, reaches 68.68% for GPT-4. The paper's "JSON and code perform comparably on tool-F1" framing (Figure 7a) is true on the metric it reports, but it obscures that under an exact-match standard, no model's code output reliably matches the reference at all.

To its credit, the paper does not rely on pass rate (executability) alone as a proxy for plan correctness — Appendix E reports both a small-scale human evaluation of execution outputs (85 examples) and an automatic evaluation using SentenceBERT/CLIP similarity and object-detection average precision against gold outputs (210 of the 882 eval queries), and finds these agree directionally with the main planning results. But because both checks run on well under a third of the 882-query evaluation set, the paper's headline claims about which configuration is "best" are ultimately validated for correctness on a small subset, not the full benchmark.

baselines

10 models spanning three open-source families at three scales (Llama-2 7B/13B/70B), a stronger open model (Llama-3-70B), a mixture-of-experts model (Mixtral-8x7B), two code-specialized models (CodeLlama-34B/70B), and three proprietary systems (Gemini-pro, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, GPT-4-0125-preview) — a reasonably broad, size-varied set for a March 2024 benchmark; GPT-4o-2024-05-13 is added as an 11th model in the camera-ready feedback table (Table 3), but only there — the strategy (Figure 5) and format (Figure 7) comparisons still rest entirely on the original early-2024 checkpoints. All are fixed, dated checkpoints.

contamination

No classic answer leakage — the dataset is freshly generated, not scraped. But GPT-4 both authored every query and rewrote the text-generation and image-generation argument values, and is also one of the evaluated planners; the paper never tests whether this self-authorship inflates GPT-4's relative standing.

what's missed

Tool-F1/argname-F1 are set-overlap scores that look far stronger than the appendix's exact full-plan-match accuracy (88.46% tool-F1 vs. 71.43% best exact plan accuracy for GPT-4; 42.27% vs. 13.83% for Llama-2-13B). Code-generation AST accuracy never exceeds 5.33% for any model despite CodeBLEU scores up to 68.68%.

would raise confidence

Report exact full-plan accuracy alongside tool-F1 in the main tables rather than burying it in the appendix; regenerate a subset of queries with a non-GPT-4 model to check for self-authorship bias; and scale the execution-output correctness check (currently 210/85 of 882 queries) to the full evaluation set.

// bottom line

m&m's is a real methodological advance over its contemporaries — it is the first tool-use benchmark to pair a fully executable, realistic 33-tool set with real multi-modal inputs at scale, letting it cleanly separate planning error from execution error and produce a genuinely useful ablation of planning strategy, plan format, and feedback. But its three headline metrics (tool-F1, argname-F1, pass rate) are all more forgiving than the stricter numbers the paper itself reports in the appendix, and the paper never examines whether using GPT-4 to both write the benchmark's queries and serve as one of its top-scoring planners could be quietly flattering GPT-4's results.

// what to remember

What to remember

  1. m&m's is a 4,427-query (882 tool-balanced, human-verified) tool-use planning benchmark built over 33 genuinely executable tools with real image/audio/text inputs — the first of its kind to let planning error and execution error be measured separately instead of conflated or emulated.
  2. Across 10 LLMs, the paper's ablation finds a consistent recipe: multi-step planning beats step-by-step on tool-F1 for every model tested (up to +21.8 points for GPT-3.5) and on pass rate for all but Gemini-pro; verification/execution feedback trades a small tool-F1 cost (under 5 points) for large pass-rate gains; and JSON format holds comparable tool-F1 to code but with a much higher pass rate.
  3. The appendix's stricter metrics tell a rockier story than the headline numbers: exact full-plan accuracy tops out at 71.43% even for GPT-4 (versus 88.46% tool-F1), and code AST accuracy never clears 5.33% for any model — a gap worth checking before trusting the main-text F1 numbers as a proxy for "solved the task."
